extensor digitorum longus: Extends the 2nd–5th toes and dorsiflexes the foot. Deep fibular nerve.
extensor hallucis brevis: Part of extensor digitorum brevis going to the big toe.
extensor hallucis longus: Extends the big toe; the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt just lateral to its tendon. It is the test muscle for the L5 root.
extensor indicis: Muscle that extends the index finger independently; often used in tendon transfers.
extensor pollicis brevis: Extends the proximal phalanx of the thumb; forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox.
extensor pollicis longus: Turns around Lister's tubercle to reach the distal phalanx of the thumb; the medial border of the snuffbox. It can rupture after a distal radius fracture.
extensor retinaculum of wrist: Band at the back of the wrist dividing the extensor tendons into six compartments.
external abdominal oblique muscle: The most superficial flat muscle of the lateral abdominal wall; its fibres run down and forwards and its lower border forms the inguinal ligament. Nerves: intercostal nerves T7–T11, subcostal nerve. It flexes the trunk and rotates it to the opposite side.
external anal sphincter: Voluntary ring of striated muscle around the anal canal; supplied by the pudendal nerve (inferior rectal nerve).
external intercostal membrane: Membranous continuation of the external intercostal muscle between the costal cartilages.
external intercostal muscles: Muscles between the ribs whose fibres run down and forwards ('hands in pockets' direction); they raise the ribs during inspiration. Intercostal nerves.
external occipital crest: Midline ridge running from the external occipital protuberance to the foramen magnum; the nuchal ligament attaches to it.
external occipital protuberance: Prominence felt in the middle of the back of the head (inion); trapezius and the nuchal ligament attach to it.
external part of thyro-arytenoid muscle: Muscle fibres that relax and shorten the vocal fold; the internal part is vocalis.
external surface of parietal bone: Outer surface of the parietal bone; the temporal lines lie on it.
external surface of squamous part of fro: Bony surface of the forehead; the frontal sinus lies beneath it.
facet for calcaneonavicular part of bifu: Facet for calcaneonavicular part of bifurcate ligament
Articular surface on the head of the talus that the bifurcate ligament touches.
facet for dens: Articular surface on the back of the anterior arch of the atlas; forms the median atlanto-axial joint with the dens.
facet for plantar calcaneonavicular liga: Articular surface of the head of the talus that rests on the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament.
fascia lata: Strong deep fascia that wraps the thigh like a stocking; laterally it forms the iliotibial band, and the great saphenous vein passes through its saphenous opening.
femur: The longest and strongest bone in the body; its head forms the hip joint with the acetabulum and its condyles the knee joint with the tibia. If the medial circumflex femoral artery is damaged in a femoral neck fracture, avascular necrosis of the head can follow.
fibrous joints of free lower limb: Fibrous joints of free lower limb
fibrous joints of free upper limb: Fibrous joints of free upper limb
fibula: Thin lateral bone of the leg; it does not bear weight but gives attachment to muscles and, through the lateral malleolus, stabilises the ankle joint. The common fibular nerve winds around its neck.
fibular articular facet: Surface of the lateral condyle that articulates with the head of the fibula.
fibular collateral ligament: Round cord from the lateral epicondyle of the femur to the fibular head; separate from the capsule and meniscus, it resists varus stress.
fibular notch: Notch at the lower end of the tibia; forms a syndesmosis with the fibula.
fibularis brevis muscle: Inserts into the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal; it everts the foot. In inversion injuries it can avulse the bone fragment it attaches to.
fibularis longus muscle: Arises from the lateral surface of the fibula and crosses the sole through the groove of the cuboid to insert into the 1st metatarsal; it everts and plantarflexes the foot. Superficial fibular nerve.
fibularis tertius muscle: Separate part of extensor digitorum longus going to the 5th metatarsal; dorsiflexes and everts the foot.
fifth metacarpal bone: The 5th of the five long bones of the metacarpus; its base articulates with the carpal bones and its head with the proximal phalanx.
fifth metatarsal bone: Metatarsal on the lateral border; fibularis brevis attaches to the tuberosity at its base, and it fractures often.
fifth rib: 5th rib: a true (vertebrosternal) rib; its cartilage joins the sternum directly.
first metacarpal bone: Metacarpal of the thumb; the shortest and thickest metacarpal, it forms a saddle joint with the trapezium.
first metatarsal bone: Thick, short metatarsal of the big toe; with the two sesamoids beneath it, it carries most of the load during walking.
first rib: 1st rib: a true (vertebrosternal) rib; its cartilage joins the sternum directly. The shortest, broadest and most curved rib; its upper surface bears the grooves for the subclavian artery and vein and the tubercle for scalenus anterior.
flexor carpi radialis: Runs from the medial epicondyle to the base of the 2nd metacarpal; flexes the hand and deviates it radially. Its tendon lies just medial to the radial pulse. Median nerve.
flexor carpi ulnaris: Inserts into the pisiform (and through the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments into the hamate and 5th metacarpal); flexes the hand and deviates it ulnarly. Ulnar nerve.
flexor digiti minimi of foot: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot
Runs from the base of the 5th metatarsal to the proximal phalanx of the little toe.
flexor digiti minimi of hand: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand
Hypothenar muscle running from the hook of the hamate to the little finger.
flexor digitorum brevis: Central superficial muscle of the sole; flexes the middle phalanges of the 2nd–5th toes.
flexor digitorum longus: Flexes the distal phalanges of the 2nd–5th toes; its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus.
flexor digitorum profundus: Runs from the ulna and interosseous membrane to the distal phalanges; the only muscle that flexes the DIP joints. Its radial half is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (median), its ulnar half by the ulnar nerve.
